title: What is positional trading, and how is it different from swing trading, intraday and investing?
summary: What positional trading means, how it differs from swing trading, intraday trading and investing, the risks, and how gains are taxed in India.
body_markdown:
## What is positional trading?


Positional trading usually means buying shares and holding them for a few weeks or months to catch a price move; swing trading usually means holding for a few days to a few weeks. These are common market terms, not SEBI terms, and the holding times are not fixed.


What makes it trading and not investing is the plan. A positional trader buys with a sale in mind: when the price move runs out, the shares go. An investor buys to own the business for years.


If you hold shares overnight in the cash market, the trade is a delivery trade. The shares are credited to your demat account, which holds your securities. You buy and sell through a trading account with a SEBI-registered stockbroker. The[stock trading basics article](https://koshex.com/blog/stock-trading-newbie-heres-what-you-should-know) explains both accounts, and how a same-day (intraday) trade differs from delivery, in more detail.


## How does positional trading work?


A trader looks for a price trend, which is a price that has been moving mostly one way for a while. They buy, hold while the trend lasts, and sell at a target price or when the trend turns.


To spot a trend, traders read price charts. This is technical analysis, and tools like moving averages (an average of recent closing prices) and support and resistance levels belong to it. Many also read a company's results, which is fundamental analysis. Neither method promises anything. They are ways of forming a view.


A trader may also place a stop-loss order. In SEBI's investor material, a stop-loss means "Sell as soon as price goes below a certain level (Trigger Price)". Until the market price reaches that trigger, the order does nothing.


Here is a made-up example with assumed prices. You buy 60 shares at ₹800, so you put in ₹48,000. Four months later you sell at ₹1,000 and receive ₹60,000. The gain is ₹12,000, which is 25% of ₹48,000.


Now the same trade going the other way. You sell at ₹700 and receive ₹42,000. The loss is ₹6,000, or 12.5% of what you put in.


## Positional, swing, intraday or long-term investing: how do they differ?


The four differ mainly in how long you hold, how you decide, where the shares sit, what it costs and how it is taxed. Intraday means buying and selling within the same trading day. The table describes shares traded in the cash market.


Intraday Swing Positional Long-term investing


Holding period Same day Days to a few weeks A few weeks or months Years


Decisions based on Price moves Price moves Trends and company results The business behind the share


Where the shares are Not delivered; the broker squares off open positions before the market closes (MIS) Your demat account (CNC, delivery) Your demat account (CNC, delivery) Your demat account (CNC, delivery)


Securities transaction tax (STT) 0.025% on the sell side 0.1% on the buy and 0.1% on the sell 0.1% on the buy and 0.1% on the sell 0.1% on the buy and 0.1% on the sell


Stamp duty, paid by the buyer 0.003% 0.015% 0.015% 0.015%


Tax on profit Speculative business income, at the income-tax rate for your income bracket Capital gain: 20% if held 12 months or less Capital gain: 20% if held 12 months or less Capital gain: 12.5% above ₹1,25,000 once held more than 12 months


Brokerage is extra on every trade. The holding times are descriptions, not rules, and a trader may hold for longer or shorter. STT, short for securities transaction tax, is a tax charged on each trade. The 20% rate applies when the sale bears STT. The 12.5% rate needs STT paid on both the purchase and the sale, with some exceptions. The ₹1,25,000 is a yearly allowance, explained below. A capital gain is the profit on selling a share or a fund unit.


For intraday, SEBI's investor material describes the MIS order type as meant for intraday trading, with positions "automatically squared off at EOD" (end of day). The CNC order type is for delivery trades, whose positions are "not automatically squared off at EOD".


## Is positional trading the same as investing?


No. A positional trader plans to sell when a trend ends, while an investor plans to keep owning for the long term. The two differ in time spent, costs and tax.


Tax is where the 12-month line matters. A listed share held for 12 months or less gives a short-term gain, taxed at 20% if the sale bears STT. Held for longer, the gain is long-term. It is taxed at 12.5% on the part above ₹1,25,000 in the tax year, when STT has been paid on buying and selling.


Take the earlier example. A ₹12,000 gain sold after four months is short-term. Tax is 20%, which is ₹2,400, plus 4% cess on that tax, which is ₹96, so ₹2,496 in all. Cess is an extra 4% charge on the tax.


Had you held the same shares for 13 months and sold at ₹1,000, the gain would be long-term. If you had no other long-term gains from shares or equity funds that year, the ₹12,000 sits inside the ₹1,25,000 allowance and there would be no tax. The allowance is one per person per tax year, shared with equity mutual funds.


## What are the risks of positional trading?


The main risk is that the trend reverses after you have bought. Holding for weeks also means you carry the position through nights and weekends, when the market is shut. A price can move while it is closed, and you can act only when it reopens. NSE's normal market runs from 09:15 to 15:30.


Other risks follow from the way the trade is built.


- **Capital stays tied up.** Money in a position cannot be used elsewhere until you sell.
- **Costs and tax eat into gains.** STT, stamp duty, brokerage and the 20% short-term tax all come off the profit.
- **Borrowed money magnifies a loss.** A margin trading facility lets a broker lend you part of the price of shares, and it can sell them if you do not top up. The[stock trading basics article](https://koshex.com/blog/stock-trading-newbie-heres-what-you-should-know) explains how it works.
- **Futures and options carry expiry and margin.** Futures and options, or F&O, are contracts that end on a set expiry date, and you post margin, a deposit, to hold them.


SEBI looked at individuals who traded equity futures and options in 2025-26. About 88 in every 100 of them ended the year with a net loss. Across all of them, the net loss came to ₹91,685 crore. A positional trade in futures or options carries that risk.


One more point. SEBI's rules do not permit naked short selling: every seller must deliver the shares at settlement. So a positional bet on a fall is made in futures or options, with the risks above.


None of this says positional trading is wrong for anyone. It says the result depends on whether the trend continues, and on costs and tax.


## How are positional trading gains taxed?


If you hold shares overnight in the cash market and sell them, the gain is a capital gain. It is 20% if you held 12 months or less and the sale bears STT. After 12 months it is 12.5% on gains above ₹1,25,000 in the tax year. That rate needs STT paid when you bought and when you sold, with some exceptions. Cess of 4% is added on top of the tax.


Losses are set off in set ways. A short-term capital loss can be used against any capital gain made in the same year, short-term or long-term. A long-term loss can be used only against long-term gains, and neither can be used against salary. A loss you could not use is carried forward for eight tax years, if you file your return by the due date.


Intraday and F&O are treated differently:


- **Intraday shares.** The profit is speculative business income, which is income from a trade, taxed at the income-tax rate for your income bracket. The Act calls a transaction speculative when it is settled without the shares actually being delivered. An intraday loss can be used only against profit from other speculative trading, and carries forward for at most four tax years. The[stock trading basics article](https://koshex.com/blog/stock-trading-newbie-heres-what-you-should-know) covers intraday tax in more detail.
- **Futures and options.** These are business income, not speculative. A business loss carries forward for eight years and cannot be set against salary.


Whether a person's own trading counts as business or as investment depends on the facts, and the Act does not settle it with a rule. For your case, ask a tax professional.


The Finance Act, 2026 raised the securities transaction tax rates on futures and options. Option sales went from 0.1% to 0.15%, exercised options from 0.125% to 0.15%, and futures from 0.02% to 0.05%.


Shares and equity funds share the same ₹1,25,000 allowance. The[mutual funds versus stocks article](https://koshex.com/blog/which-is-better-mutual-funds-or-stocks) goes through that in more detail.


## What if you want to hold for years without watching charts?


An equity mutual fund holds shares for you. SEBI defines an equity scheme as one that mainly invests in equity and equity related instruments. A fund manager chooses and changes the holdings under SEBI's rules.


A SEBI-registered mutual fund's own income is exempt from tax. So trades inside the fund create no tax for you until you sell your units.


The risk does not go away. A fund that is fully invested in shares reads High at best on the riskometer, and usually Very High. The riskometer is the risk label SEBI makes every fund show, on six levels from Low to Very High. A fall in the market is a fall in the fund.


You can read about[equity funds](https://koshex.com/mutual-funds/categories/equity-funds) and[index funds](https://koshex.com/mutual-funds/categories/index-funds) on their category pages.
